explanation: Peopleware tells me what lets a team jell; Lencioni tells me what’s missing when it doesn’t. Read together, they say the same thing from two sides: results come from the human conditions, not the process.
Autonomy without candor drifts. I give people control over the how, and Scott’s care-and-challenge feedback is how they find out whether it’s working.
Larson scales the organization; Fournier scales the leader. Growing a team well needs both: the structure has to change, and so does the person running it.
XP’s discipline only holds on Peopleware’s foundation. Sustainable pace and protected focus aren’t perks; they’re what keeps tests written and builds green.
These two argue with each other. Greene maps manipulative insincerity in detail; Scott names it the worst quadrant. I read Greene to recognize the moves and Scott to know what to do instead.
Stanier is the daily craft of running one team; Fournier is how that craft has to change on every rung above it. Start with Stanier, then keep Fournier for each promotion.
Autonomy works on a leash, and XP is the leash: tests and CI define the boundary, and inside it engineers (and agents) get real freedom to change the code.

A tension worth holding: Lencioni treats team failure as behavior, Larson as structure. When accountability is missing I check both, starting with the system, because a structural problem looks like a people problem from the inside.
Greene’s tactics are a recipe for Lencioni’s base dysfunction. Concealing intentions and guarding position destroy the trust everything else is built on.
XP described the practices: small releases, tests first, continuous integration. Accelerate brought the evidence that they pay off at scale. I read Beck for the how and Forsgren for the proof.
Larson tells me what state a team is in; Accelerate gives me four numbers to check whether my fix is working. Together they turn org design from opinion into an experiment.
Clean Code is the craft inside XP’s practices. Refactoring, simple design and tests only work if the code is readable enough to change safely.

They disagree about where quality comes from. Martin puts it in the individual’s craft; Accelerate puts it in the system of capabilities. I side with the system, then use craft as the standard the system enforces.
